transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi… thanks for seeing me. I guess what made me call EAP was, um, I’ve been getting really jumpy at work. Like little bangs in the office — a file drawer shutting, or someone dropping a coffee mug — I kind of jump hard, more than I should. And then my chest keeps racing for a while after. It’s probably not a huge thing, but it’s been noticeable enough that I thought I should come in.
Are there any specific situations or things that you think might be causing you to feel jumpy?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but it’s mostly sudden noises at work. Like if a file drawer slams shut or somebody drops a mug, I jump really hard. More than seems normal, I guess. And then my chest keeps racing for a while after, which is what made me think maybe I should call EAP.
Are you experiencing these jumpy feelings and racing chest all the time, or just when you're at work?

Mostly at work, I think. I’m not walking around like that all day or anything. It’s just those sudden little bangs in the office — like a drawer shutting or someone dropping a mug — I jump way harder than I’d expect, and then my chest keeps racing longer than it probably should. I mean, I know that might sound kind of minor, but it’s been enough that I noticed it.
Do you feel anxious or on edge when you're not at work?

Not really as much when I’m away from work, no. It’s more in the office… I mean, I wouldn’t say I’m panicking or anything. But I’ve noticed I keep checking where my boss is, where the exits are, and if anyone’s coming up behind me, even when I’m supposed to be focused on my team. It feels a little silly saying it out loud, but that’s kind of what’s been happening.
Have you ever had a sudden feeling of intense fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes?

I don’t think so… not like, out of nowhere where it suddenly peaks in a few minutes. I mean, I get startled and my body reacts, but I wouldn’t want to call it an intense fear thing unless that’s what you mean. It feels more like I’m caught off guard than having an attack or something.
Do you feel anxious in other situations, like when you're in crowded places or public transportation?

Not really, no. Crowds and buses or the train don’t really do that to me, at least not that I’ve noticed. I mean, I might be a little more aware of people than usual, but I wouldn’t say I’m anxious in those situations. Does that make sense?
Is there anything about your work or job that you think might be contributing to how you're feeling?

Yeah, I think so. It’s probably connected to work, honestly. This has really only been going on for about two weeks, since that late-night confrontation with my regional boss. I don’t want to make it sound bigger than it is, but that’s when I started noticing it.
Is the anxiety you're experiencing at work related to the confrontation with your regional boss or is it more about the work environment in general?

I think it’s more tied to that confrontation, honestly. I don’t want to overstate it, but it’s been about two weeks now, and it really seemed to start after that late-night thing with my regional boss. Before that, I wouldn’t have said the work environment in general was making me feel this way.
Are you afraid of the noise itself or is it more about what the noise might mean or lead to in the work context?

I guess it’s not the noise itself, exactly. Like, I know a file drawer slamming or someone dropping a coffee mug isn’t dangerous. But lately every little bang at the office makes me jump way more than it should, and then my chest keeps racing for a while after. That’s actually part of why I called EAP… I felt kind of silly about it, but it was starting to bother me.
Do you think you would have this jumpy reaction to sudden noises in other environments outside of your workplace?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I’ve mostly noticed it at work. Like, every little bang in the office—a file drawer shutting, someone dropping a coffee mug—makes me jump harder than I should, and then my chest keeps racing for longer than seems normal. I don’t know if I’d react the same way somewhere else, but that’s where it’s been happening enough that I finally called EAP.
Do you think you would react the same way to sudden noises if you were in a different job or work setting?

I think… probably, if it felt similar enough. I don’t want to make it sound bigger than it is, but what made me call EAP was that in the office, every little bang—like a file drawer shutting or someone dropping a coffee mug—makes me jump hard, and then my chest keeps racing way longer than it should. So in a different job setting, I guess if there were sudden noises like that, I might react the same way.
Do you think you would react the same way to sudden noises, like a loud bang, if you were at home or with friends?

I don’t know, maybe not as much? I mean, I haven’t really noticed it at home or with friends the same way. The thing that stood out enough for me to call EAP was at the office—just little bangs, like a file drawer shutting or somebody dropping a mug, and I jump hard, then my chest keeps racing longer than it should. I’m not trying to overstate it, but that’s where I’ve really noticed it.
Do you think you would have the same reaction to sudden noises if you were not thinking about work or your job at the time?

I’m not sure, to be honest. I don’t want to make too much of it, but the main thing is what’s been happening at the office. Even small bangs, like a file drawer shutting or someone dropping a coffee mug, make me jump really hard, and then my chest keeps racing longer than it should. If I wasn’t thinking about work at all, maybe it wouldn’t be as bad… but I’m not totally sure.
Do you think your jumpy reaction to sudden noises would stop if you were to change jobs or work in a different office?

I’d like to think it would, yeah… but I’m not totally sure. What really made me call EAP was that in the office, every little bang—like a file drawer closing or someone dropping a coffee mug—makes me jump harder than I think it should, and then my chest keeps racing for a while. So maybe a different office or job would help if it didn’t have that same kind of noise, but I don’t know if it would completely stop.
Do you think your jumpy reaction to sudden noises would happen if you were working in a completely different field or industry?

I guess it might be less tied to the industry itself and more to being in that office setting, if that makes sense. I don’t want to sound dramatic, but what pushed me to call EAP was that every little bang at work—like a file drawer shutting or someone dropping a coffee mug—makes me jump pretty hard, and then my chest keeps racing way longer than it should. So in a totally different field… maybe it would still happen if the environment felt the same? I’m not completely sure.
Do you think your jumpy reaction to sudden noises would still happen if you were to work in the same office but in a different role?

Yeah… I think it probably would, honestly. I don’t know that the role is the main thing. It’s more that in that same office, every little bang—like a file drawer shutting or someone dropping a coffee mug—makes me jump really hard, and then my chest keeps racing longer than it should. That’s actually what made me call EAP. I know it might sound like a small thing, but it’s been hard to shake.
Do you think your jumpy reaction to sudden noises would still happen if you were working in a similar office setting, but not the exact same one you're in now?

Yeah, I think… probably, yes. I mean, I don’t want to overstate it, because maybe a different office would be calmer or I’d get used to it. But what made me call EAP was that in the office, every little bang—like a file drawer shutting or someone dropping a coffee mug—makes me jump hard, and then my chest keeps racing way longer than it should. So if it was a similar kind of office, I’d be worried it would still happen.
Do you think you would have the same jumpy reaction to sudden noises if you were to work in a completely different office?

I think… yeah, maybe I would. I don’t want to make it sound like it’s every single noise or that I can’t function, but what bothered me enough to call EAP was that little sudden bangs in an office — like a file drawer shutting or someone dropping a coffee mug — make me jump really hard. And then my chest keeps racing for a while after, longer than seems normal. So even in a completely different office, I’d be worried it could still happen.
Do you think your jumpy reaction to sudden noises would still happen if you were to work in a completely quiet office?

If it was completely quiet, I guess it might be better… I don’t want to make it sound like I’m just reacting to nothing. It’s really the sudden little bangs that get me — like a file drawer slamming shut or someone dropping a mug. That’s what made me call EAP, because I jump harder than I think I should, and then my chest keeps racing for way too long after. So in a truly quiet office, maybe it wouldn’t happen as much… as long as there weren’t those sudden noises.
Do you think you would have the same jumpy reaction to sudden noises if you were to work in a different company?

Yeah, I think it could, honestly. I mean, I’d like to think a different company might feel different and maybe I’d settle in better, but it’s the sudden noises themselves that seem to set me off. Like every little bang in the office — a file drawer shutting, somebody dropping a coffee mug — I jump really hard, and then my chest keeps racing way longer than it should. That’s what made me call EAP in the first place, if that makes sense.
